--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [DataScan.summary_data]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} | Pointblank description: The column statistics as a DataFrame. twitter-card: title: >- [DataScan.summary_data]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} | Pointblank description: The column statistics as a DataFrame. title: >- [DataScan.summary_data]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: The column statistics as a DataFrame. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} The column statistics as a DataFrame. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [DataScan.summary_data]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} The report from [`get_tabular_report()`](`pointblank.DataScan.get_tabular_report`) is for reading, while `summary_data` holds the same statistics as data. That's useful for finding columns that need attention (the ones with missing values, or with a single distinct value), for building validation steps from what was found, or for passing the profile to another tool. The statistics are described in the [`DataScan`](`pointblank.DataScan`) documentation. A statistic that doesn't apply to a column's type is null (for example, `mean` for a date column). The order of the statistic columns isn't fixed, so select columns by name. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Here's the summary for the numeric columns of the `small_table` dataset. ::: {#bb2c8a51 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import polars as pl small_table = pb.load_dataset(dataset="small_table", tbl_type="polars") summary = pb.DataScan(small_table).summary_data ( summary .filter(pl.col("coltype").is_in(["Int64", "Float64"])) .select("colname", "n_missing", "n_unique", "mean", "min", "max") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 6)
colnamen_missingn_uniquemeanminmax
stri64i64f64strstr
"a"073.769231"1""8"
"c"275.727273"2""9"
"d"0122304.702308"108.34""9999.99"
``` ::: ::: Column `c` is the only one with missing values. The `min` and `max` columns are strings, because they also hold the dates from the date columns. Since this is an ordinary DataFrame, the profile can lead to further checks. This finds the columns with one distinct value fewer than the table has rows: ::: {#71c65094 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} summary.filter(pl.col("n_unique") == small_table.height - 1).get_column("colname").to_list() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['date_time', 'b', 'd'] ``` ::: ::: Three columns that look like they should identify each row (a timestamp, a code, and an amount) each have exactly one repeated value. That's a sign of a duplicated row, which [`Validate.rows_distinct()`](`pointblank.Validate.rows_distinct`) would confirm.
